stem: is a liquid at room temperature.
solution:
**Mercury.**

Every other metal is a solid at room temperature; mercury is the one exception, which is why it is the metal used in thermometers.

subtopic: Physical Properties of Metals and Non-metals
stem: Explain the meanings of malleable and ductile.
solution:
**Malleable.** A substance is malleable if it can be **beaten into thin sheets** without breaking. Metals are malleable as a class, and **gold and silver are the most malleable** of them.

**Ductile.** A substance is ductile if it can be **drawn into thin wires**. **Gold is the most ductile metal** — a wire about 2 km long can be drawn from a single gram of it.

It is because metals are both malleable and ductile that they can be given whatever shape a use calls for.
groundedIn: §3.1.1 Metals, with Activity 3.3 (malleability) and Activity 3.4 (ductility), which give both definitions and both superlatives.

stem: Why is sodium kept immersed in kerosene oil?
solution:
Sodium is **so reactive towards oxygen that it catches fire if left in the open**. Potassium behaves the same way.

Kerosene keeps air and moisture off the metal surface, so the sodium can neither react with the oxygen of the air nor react violently with water vapour. Storing it under kerosene both protects the metal and **prevents accidental fires**.
groundedIn: §3.2.1 What happens when Metals are burnt in Air?, which states that potassium and sodium react so vigorously that they catch fire if kept in the open and are therefore kept immersed in kerosene oil.

context: Write equations for the reactions of
stem: iron with steam
solution:
Iron does not react with cold or hot water, but it **does react with steam**, giving the oxide and hydrogen:

\(3\text{Fe}(s) + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \rightarrow \text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4(s) + 4\text{H}_2(g)\)
groundedIn: §3.2.2 What happens when Metals react with Water?, with Activity 3.10 and Fig. 3.3 — metals react with water to give a metal oxide (or hydroxide) and hydrogen, and the section gives the potassium, sodium, calcium and steam reactions explicitly.

context: Write equations for the reactions of
stem: calcium and potassium with water
solution:
**Calcium with water.** The reaction is less violent than potassium's — the heat evolved is not enough for the hydrogen to catch fire:

\(\text{Ca}(s) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)\)

The calcium starts floating, because bubbles of hydrogen stick to its surface.

**Potassium with water.** Violent and strongly exothermic — the hydrogen evolved catches fire at once:

\(2\text{K}(s) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow 2\text{KOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2(g) + \text{heat energy}\)
groundedIn: §3.2.2 What happens when Metals react with Water?, with Activity 3.10 and Fig. 3.3 — metals react with water to give a metal oxide (or hydroxide) and hydrogen, and the section gives the potassium, sodium, calcium and steam reactions explicitly.

Samples of four metals A, B, C and D were taken and added to the following solutions one by one. The results obtained have been tabulated as follows.

| Metal | Iron(II) sulphate | Copper(II) sulphate | Zinc sulphate | Silver nitrate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | No reaction | Displacement | — | — |
| B | Displacement | — | No reaction | — |
| C | No reaction | No reaction | No reaction | Displacement |
| D | No reaction | No reaction | No reaction | No reaction |

(A dash marks a cell the book leaves blank.) Use the table above to answer the following questions about metals A, B, C and D.
stem: Which is the most reactive metal?
solution:
**B is the most reactive.**

Read each result as a comparison:

- **B** displaces iron from iron(II) sulphate, so **B is more reactive than iron**. It does not react with zinc sulphate, so it is **less reactive than zinc**. That places B between zinc and iron.
- **A** does not displace iron, so it is **less reactive than iron**, but it does displace copper, so it is **more reactive than copper**.
- **C** displaces only silver, so it sits **below copper and above silver**.
- **D** displaces nothing at all, not even silver, so it is **the least reactive**.

B is the only metal that outranks iron, so B is the most reactive of the four.
groundedIn: §3.2.4 How do Metals react with Solutions of other Metal Salts? and §3.2.5 The Reactivity Series with Table 3.2 — if metal A displaces metal B from its solution it is the more reactive of the two, and Table 3.2 orders K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au.

stem: What would you observe if B is added to a solution of Copper(II) sulphate?
solution:
**A displacement reaction takes place.** B is more reactive than iron, and iron is more reactive than copper, so B is more reactive than copper and displaces it from the solution.

What you would see:

- The **blue colour of the copper(II) sulphate solution fades**, as the copper ions leave it.
- A **reddish-brown deposit of copper** collects on the surface of B.
groundedIn: §3.2.4 How do Metals react with Solutions of other Metal Salts? and §3.2.5 The Reactivity Series with Table 3.2 — if metal A displaces metal B from its solution it is the more reactive of the two, and Table 3.2 orders K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au.

stem: Arrange the metals A, B, C and D in the order of decreasing reactivity.
solution:
**B \(>\) A \(>\) C \(>\) D**

- **B** is above iron (it displaces iron).
- **A** is below iron but above copper (it fails with iron, succeeds with copper).
- **C** is below copper but above silver (it fails with copper, succeeds with silver).
- **D** fails even with silver nitrate, so it is below silver and least reactive of all.
groundedIn: §3.2.4 How do Metals react with Solutions of other Metal Salts? and §3.2.5 The Reactivity Series with Table 3.2 — if metal A displaces metal B from its solution it is the more reactive of the two, and Table 3.2 orders K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au.

stem: Which gas is produced when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a reactive metal? Write the chemical reaction when iron reacts with dilute H₂SO₄.
solution:
**Hydrogen gas** is produced. A metal above hydrogen in the activity series displaces it from a dilute acid:

Metal + Dilute acid \(\rightarrow\) Salt + Hydrogen

**Iron with dilute sulphuric acid:**

\(\text{Fe}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{FeSO}_4(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)\)

Dilute acid gives iron(II) sulphate, so the iron here is in the \(+2\) state.
groundedIn: §3.2.3 What happens when Metals react with Acids?, which gives the general form metal + dilute acid → salt + hydrogen, with Activity 3.11 and Table 3.2 for which metals lie above hydrogen.

stem: What would you observe when zinc is added to a solution of iron(II) sulphate? Write the chemical reaction that takes place.
solution:
**Zinc is more reactive than iron**, so it displaces iron from the solution.

What you would see:

- The **pale green colour of the iron(II) sulphate solution fades**, since the iron ions are leaving it.
- A **greyish-black deposit of iron** collects on the zinc.

\(\text{Zn}(s) + \text{FeSO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{ZnSO}_4(aq) + \text{Fe}(s)\)

This is a **displacement reaction**.
groundedIn: §3.2.4 How do Metals react with Solutions of other Metal Salts? with Activity 3.12 and Fig. 3.4 — a reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt solution — and Table 3.2, which places zinc above iron.

context: Answer the following about the formation and nature of ionic compounds.
stem: Write the electron-dot structures for sodium, oxygen and magnesium.
solution:
Each structure shows only the **valence (outermost) electrons** as dots around the symbol.

- **Sodium**, \(\text{Na}\) (2,8,1) — one valence electron, so **Na** with a single dot beside it.
- **Magnesium**, \(\text{Mg}\) (2,8,2) — two valence electrons, so **Mg** with two dots beside it.
- **Oxygen**, \(\text{O}\) (2,6) — six valence electrons, so **O** surrounded by six dots, drawn as two pairs and two single dots.
groundedIn: §3.3 How do Metals and Non-metals React? with Table 3.3 and Figs. 3.5 and 3.6 — a metal atom loses its valence electrons to attain a noble-gas configuration and a non-metal atom gains them, and the oppositely charged ions are then held by strong electrostatic forces.

context: Answer the following about the formation and nature of ionic compounds.
stem: Show the formation of Na₂O and MgO by the transfer of electrons.
solution:
In both cases the metal **gives up** its valence electrons and oxygen **takes** them, and both partners end with a stable octet.

**Sodium oxide, \(\text{Na}_2\text{O}\).** Each sodium atom has one electron to give and oxygen needs two, so **two sodium atoms** are required for one oxygen atom:

\(2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{Na}^+ + 2e^-\)

\(\text{O} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{O}^{2-}\)

giving \(2\text{Na}^+ + \text{O}^{2-} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{O}\)

**Magnesium oxide, \(\text{MgO}\).** Magnesium has two electrons to give and oxygen needs exactly two, so they pair **one to one**:

\(\text{Mg} \rightarrow \text{Mg}^{2+} + 2e^-\)

\(\text{O} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{O}^{2-}\)

giving \(\text{Mg}^{2+} + \text{O}^{2-} \rightarrow \text{MgO}\)
groundedIn: §3.3 How do Metals and Non-metals React? with Table 3.3 and Figs. 3.5 and 3.6 — a metal atom loses its valence electrons to attain a noble-gas configuration and a non-metal atom gains them, and the oppositely charged ions are then held by strong electrostatic forces.

context: Answer the following about the formation and nature of ionic compounds.
stem: What are the ions present in these compounds?
solution:
- **Sodium oxide, \(\text{Na}_2\text{O}\)** — two sodium ions \(\text{Na}^+\) and one oxide ion \(\text{O}^{2-}\).
- **Magnesium oxide, \(\text{MgO}\)** — one magnesium ion \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) and one oxide ion \(\text{O}^{2-}\).

In each compound the total positive charge balances the total negative charge, so the compound as a whole is neutral.
groundedIn: §3.3 How do Metals and Non-metals React? with Table 3.3 and Figs. 3.5 and 3.6 — a metal atom loses its valence electrons to attain a noble-gas configuration and a non-metal atom gains them, and the oppositely charged ions are then held by strong electrostatic forces.

stem: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
solution:
An ionic compound is built of **oppositely charged ions packed together and held by strong electrostatic forces of attraction**.

Melting means breaking that rigid arrangement apart so the ions can move. Because the inter-ionic attraction is strong, a **considerable amount of energy** is needed to overcome it — and that energy has to be supplied as heat. Hence the high melting points (and, for the same reason, high boiling points).
groundedIn: §3.3.1 Properties of Ionic Compounds, item (ii) Melting and Boiling points, with Table 3.4 — a considerable amount of energy is required to break the strong inter-ionic attraction.

context: Define the following terms.
stem: Mineral
solution:
**A mineral is an element or a compound that occurs naturally in the earth's crust.**

Every ore is a mineral, but most minerals are not ores — the extra condition is in the next definition.
groundedIn: §3.4 Occurrence of Metals and §3.4.2 Enrichment of Ores — minerals are the elements or compounds occurring naturally in the earth's crust, ores are those minerals from which a metal can be profitably extracted, and gangue is the soil and sand contaminating a mined ore.

context: Define the following terms.
stem: Ore
solution:
**An ore is a mineral that contains a high enough percentage of a particular metal for the metal to be extracted from it profitably.**

The test is economic as much as chemical: a mineral holding a metal in too small a proportion to be worth extracting is not called an ore.
groundedIn: §3.4 Occurrence of Metals and §3.4.2 Enrichment of Ores — minerals are the elements or compounds occurring naturally in the earth's crust, ores are those minerals from which a metal can be profitably extracted, and gangue is the soil and sand contaminating a mined ore.

context: Define the following terms.
stem: Gangue
solution:
**Gangue is the unwanted impurity — soil, sand and the like — that contaminates an ore as it is mined.**

It must be removed before the metal is extracted. The separation techniques used exploit the differences between the physical or chemical properties of the gangue and of the ore.
groundedIn: §3.4 Occurrence of Metals and §3.4.2 Enrichment of Ores — minerals are the elements or compounds occurring naturally in the earth's crust, ores are those minerals from which a metal can be profitably extracted, and gangue is the soil and sand contaminating a mined ore.

stem: Name two metals which are found in nature in the free state.
solution:
**Gold and silver.**

Platinum and copper are equally correct answers. These metals sit at the **bottom of the activity series**, so they are too unreactive to have combined with other elements, and are found uncombined — in the native or free state.
groundedIn: §3.4.1 Extraction of Metals, which records that gold, silver, platinum and copper are found in the free state, and Fig. 3.9, which marks the least reactive metals as found in the native state.

stem: What chemical process is used for obtaining a metal from its oxide?
solution:
**Reduction.** Obtaining a metal from its compound is a reduction process, because the metal ion gains electrons and the oxygen is removed.

Which reducing agent is used depends on where the metal sits in the activity series:

- **Metals in the middle** (zinc, iron, lead) — their oxides are reduced by heating with **carbon**: \(\text{ZnO}(s) + \text{C}(s) \rightarrow \text{Zn}(s) + \text{CO}(g)\).
- **Metals at the top** (sodium, magnesium, calcium, aluminium) — carbon cannot reduce their oxides, because these metals have a greater affinity for oxygen than carbon does. They are obtained by **electrolytic reduction**.
groundedIn: §3.4.4 Extracting Metals in the Middle of the Activity Series (reduction with carbon) and §3.4.5 Extracting Metals towards the Top of the Activity Series (electrolytic reduction).

context:
Metallic oxides of zinc, magnesium and copper were heated with the following metals.

| Metal → | Zinc | Magnesium | Copper |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zinc oxide | | | |
| Magnesium oxide | | | |
| Copper oxide | | | |

(The book prints this grid empty, for the reader to fill in.)
stem: In which cases will you find displacement reactions taking place?
solution:
A metal displaces another metal from its oxide only if it is **more reactive** than that metal. From the activity series, **magnesium \(>\) zinc \(>\) copper**.

Filling the grid — **D** marks a displacement, **N** no reaction:

| Oxide heated with → | Zinc | Magnesium | Copper |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zinc oxide | N | **D** | N |
| Magnesium oxide | N | N | N |
| Copper oxide | **D** | **D** | N |

So displacement occurs in **three** cases:

- **Zinc oxide + magnesium**: \(\text{ZnO} + \text{Mg} \rightarrow \text{MgO} + \text{Zn}\)
- **Copper oxide + zinc**: \(\text{CuO} + \text{Zn} \rightarrow \text{ZnO} + \text{Cu}\)
- **Copper oxide + magnesium**: \(\text{CuO} + \text{Mg} \rightarrow \text{MgO} + \text{Cu}\)

Every other cell is no reaction: magnesium oxide cannot be reduced by either of the less reactive metals, and a metal cannot displace itself from its own oxide.
groundedIn: §3.2.5 The Reactivity Series with Table 3.2, which orders Mg above Zn above Cu, read with §3.2.4 — a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound.

stem: Which metals do not corrode easily?
solution:
**Gold and platinum**, and to a large extent **silver**.

These are the metals at the **bottom of the activity series**. Corrosion is a reaction with the air and moisture around the metal, so the less reactive the metal, the less readily it corrodes — gold and platinum do not react with oxygen even at high temperatures, which is also why they are found in nature in the free state.

Silver does eventually tarnish, turning black as it reacts with the sulphur in the air, but it resists corrosion far better than iron.
groundedIn: §3.5 Corrosion, which lists what happens to silver, copper and iron on exposure to air, read with §3.2.1, where silver and gold are recorded as not reacting with oxygen even at high temperatures.

stem: What are alloys?
solution:
**An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal and a non-metal.**

It is made by melting the primary metal first, dissolving the other elements in it in definite proportions, and then cooling the mixture to room temperature. If one of the metals is **mercury**, the alloy is called an **amalgam**.

Alloying changes a metal's properties for the better — pure iron is soft and stretches when hot, but iron with about 0.05% carbon is hard and strong, and iron with nickel and chromium gives **stainless steel**, which is hard and does not rust.
groundedIn: §3.5.1 Prevention of Corrosion, which defines an alloy, names the amalgam case and gives the iron-carbon and stainless-steel examples.

stem: Which of the following pairs will give displacement reactions?
solution:
A displacement happens only when the **added metal is more reactive than the metal already in solution**. Reading each pair against the activity series (K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au):

- (A) Copper into sodium chloride — copper is far **below** sodium. No reaction.
- (B) Aluminium into magnesium chloride — aluminium is **below** magnesium. No reaction.
- (C) Silver into iron(II) sulphate — silver is **below** iron. No reaction.
- **(D) Copper into silver nitrate** — copper is **above** silver, so it displaces silver: \(\text{Cu}(s) + 2\text{AgNO}_3(aq) \rightarrow \text{Cu(NO}_3)_2(aq) + 2\text{Ag}(s)\).
groundedIn: §3.2.5 The Reactivity Series with Table 3.2, read with §3.2.4 — a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution.

stem: Which of the following methods is suitable for preventing an iron frying pan from rusting?
solution:
Iron rusts only where **both air and water** reach its surface, so anything that keeps them off works.

- (A) Grease forms a barrier layer.
- (B) Paint forms a barrier layer.
- (C) A coating of zinc is **galvanisation**, and it protects the article even if the coating gets broken.

All three are listed by the book as ways of preventing rusting, so the answer is **(D) All of the above**.

In practice grease and paint would be poor choices for a *frying pan*, which is heated and scoured — but the question asks which methods prevent rusting, and each of them does.
groundedIn: §3.5.1 Prevention of Corrosion, which lists painting, oiling, greasing, galvanising, chrome plating, anodising and alloying, and Activity 3.14 with Fig. 3.13 for the air-and-water condition.

stem: An element reacts with oxygen to give a compound with a high melting point. This compound is also soluble in water. The element is likely to be
solution:
Two clues point the same way.

- A **high melting point** means the oxide is **ionic**, and ionic oxides are formed by **metals**.
- **Soluble in water** narrows it further: most metal oxides are insoluble, but the oxides of the most reactive metals dissolve to give alkalis.

- **(A) Calcium** is a reactive metal; calcium oxide has a high melting point and dissolves in water to give calcium hydroxide. This fits both clues.
- (B) Carbon and (C) silicon are **non-metals**, whose oxides are acidic; carbon dioxide is a gas, so no high melting point.
- (D) Iron forms oxides with high melting points, but they are **insoluble in water**.
groundedIn: §3.2.1 What happens when Metals are burnt in Air? — most metal oxides are insoluble in water but some dissolve to form alkalis — read with §3.3.1, which gives ionic compounds their high melting points, and the p39 note that non-metal oxides are acidic.

stem: Food cans are coated with tin and not with zinc because

options.label: B
options.text: zinc has a higher melting point than tin

options.label: C
options.text: zinc is more reactive than tin

options.label: D
options.text: zinc is less reactive than tin

solution:
A can holds food, much of which is acidic. The coating must be the **less** reactive metal, or it will react with the food.

**Zinc is more reactive than tin**, so a zinc lining would react with the acids in the food and contaminate it. Tin is much less reactive, so it stays inert against the contents — hence **(C)**.

- (A) is the wrong way round: tin is the costlier metal.
- (B) is false, and melting point is not what decides this anyway.
- (D) states the reactivity backwards.
groundedIn: §3.2.5 The Reactivity Series with Table 3.2, which places zinc well above tin's neighbourhood in the series, read with §3.2.3 on metals reacting with acids.

subtopic: Physical Properties of Metals and Non-metals
context: You are given a hammer, a battery, a bulb, wires and a switch.
stem: How could you use them to distinguish between samples of metals and non-metals?
solution:
**Test 1 — the hammer (malleability).** Place the sample on a hard surface and strike it with the hammer.

- A **metal** flattens into a sheet, because metals are malleable.
- A **non-metal** is brittle and **breaks into pieces**.

**Test 2 — the circuit (electrical conductivity).** Connect the battery, bulb and switch in series with two free ends, and clip the sample between those ends. Close the switch.

- The bulb **glows** for a **metal**, which is a good conductor of electricity.
- The bulb **stays dark** for a **non-metal**, which is a bad conductor.
groundedIn: Activity 3.3 (striking metals with a hammer) and Activity 3.6 with Fig. 3.2 (the conductivity circuit), both in §3.1.1, with §3.1.2 for the non-metal comparison.

subtopic: Physical Properties of Metals and Non-metals
context: You are given a hammer, a battery, a bulb, wires and a switch.
stem: Assess the usefulness of these tests in distinguishing between metals and non-metals.
solution:
The two tests together are a **useful first sort, but they are not conclusive**, because the physical properties they measure have real exceptions.

**Where they work.** For the common samples — iron, copper, aluminium against sulphur and coal — both tests agree and the classification is clear. Using **two** tests is better than one, since an element has to fail both to be misread.

**Where they fail.**

- **Graphite**, an allotrope of the non-metal carbon, **conducts electricity**, so the circuit test would wrongly call it a metal.
- The hammer test needs a **solid** sample, so it says nothing about the many non-metals that are gases, or about bromine, which is a liquid.
- Some metals are themselves awkward: sodium is so soft it would simply squash, and mercury is a liquid.

This is why the book concludes that elements **cannot be grouped by physical properties alone** — the reliable classification is by chemical properties.
groundedIn: §3.1.2 Non-metals and Table 3.1, where the book states that we cannot group elements according to their physical properties alone and lists the exceptions — mercury a liquid, iodine lustrous, graphite a conductor, the alkali metals soft.

stem: What are amphoteric oxides? Give two examples of amphoteric oxides.
solution:
**Amphoteric oxides are metal oxides that react with both acids and bases to produce a salt and water.** Most metal oxides are simply basic; these behave both ways.

**Two examples: aluminium oxide \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\) and zinc oxide \(\text{ZnO}\).**

Aluminium oxide shows both behaviours:

With an acid — \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 6\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{AlCl}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

With a base — \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow 2\text{NaAlO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\) (sodium aluminate)
groundedIn: §3.2.1 What happens when Metals are burnt in Air?, which defines amphoteric oxides, names aluminium oxide and zinc oxide, and gives both aluminium oxide equations.

stem: Name two metals which will displace hydrogen from dilute acids, and two metals which will not.
solution:
The dividing line is **hydrogen's own position in the activity series**: a metal above hydrogen displaces it from a dilute acid, a metal below it does not.

**Will displace hydrogen: magnesium and zinc.** Both lie above hydrogen, so they give hydrogen gas with dilute acid — for example

\(\text{Mg}(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)\)

Aluminium and iron would do as well.

**Will not displace hydrogen: copper and silver.** Both lie below hydrogen. Copper produced no bubbles at all with dilute hydrochloric acid, and its temperature did not change. Gold and mercury are equally acceptable answers.
groundedIn: §3.2.3 What happens when Metals react with Acids? with Activity 3.11 — the reactivity order Mg > Al > Zn > Fe and the finding that copper does not react with dilute HCl — and Table 3.2, which places [H] between lead and copper.

stem: In the electrolytic refining of a metal M, what would you take as the anode, the cathode and the electrolyte?
solution:
- **Anode** — a thick block of the **impure metal M**.
- **Cathode** — a thin strip of **pure metal M**.
- **Electrolyte** — a solution of a **soluble salt of M**, acidified (for copper the book uses acidified copper sulphate solution).

On passing the current, metal M dissolves off the anode into the electrolyte and an equal amount of **pure M is deposited on the cathode**. The **soluble impurities go into the solution**, while the **insoluble impurities settle below the anode as anode mud**.
groundedIn: §3.4.6 Refining of Metals with Fig. 3.12, whose caption gives the arrangement for copper — acidified copper sulphate as electrolyte, impure copper as anode, a strip of pure copper as cathode — and the anode-mud paragraph that follows it.

context: Pratyush took sulphur powder on a spatula and heated it. He collected the gas evolved by inverting a test tube over it.
stem: What will be the action of the gas on (i) dry litmus paper? (ii) moist litmus paper?
solution:
The gas is **sulphur dioxide**, \(\text{SO}_2\) — the oxide of a non-metal, and therefore acidic.

**(i) Dry litmus paper — no change.** An acidic gas shows its acidic character only through \(\text{H}^+\) ions, and those appear only in water. With no moisture anywhere, no ions form and the colour does not change.

**(ii) Moist litmus paper — blue litmus turns red.** The water on the paper dissolves the gas to form sulphurous acid, which releases \(\text{H}^+\) ions:

\(\text{SO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{SO}_3(aq)\)
groundedIn: §3.2.1 and the p39 conclusion that most non-metals produce acidic oxides when dissolved in water, read with Activity 3.8, which burns sulphur, collects the fumes in a test tube, adds water and tests the solution with litmus — the water in that step is what makes the litmus respond at all.

context: Pratyush took sulphur powder on a spatula and heated it. He collected the gas evolved by inverting a test tube over it.
stem: Write a balanced chemical equation for the reaction taking place.
solution:
Sulphur burns in air to give sulphur dioxide:

\(\text{S}(s) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{SO}_2(g)\)

The equation is already balanced as written — one sulphur atom and two oxygen atoms on each side.
groundedIn: §3.2.1 and the p39 conclusion that most non-metals produce acidic oxides when dissolved in water, read with Activity 3.8, which burns sulphur, collects the fumes in a test tube, adds water and tests the solution with litmus — the water in that step is what makes the litmus respond at all.

stem: State two ways to prevent the rusting of iron.
solution:
Iron rusts only where **both air and water** reach its surface, so every method works by keeping one of them away or by changing the metal itself.

**1. Galvanisation.** Coat the iron or steel with a thin layer of **zinc**. This is the better of the two, because the galvanised article stays protected **even if the zinc coating is broken**.

**2. Painting (or oiling and greasing).** A continuous layer of paint, oil or grease seals the surface off from air and moisture.

Chrome plating, anodising and alloying — mixing iron with nickel and chromium to make stainless steel — are equally acceptable answers.
groundedIn: §3.5.1 Prevention of Corrosion, which lists the methods and explains galvanisation, with Activity 3.14 and Fig. 3.13 for the air-and-water condition.

stem: What type of oxides are formed when non-metals combine with oxygen?
solution:
**Acidic oxides**, and a few **neutral** ones.

Most non-metal oxides dissolve in water to give acids — burning sulphur gives \(\text{SO}_2\), which dissolves to form sulphurous acid and turns blue litmus red. This is the opposite of what metals do: metal oxides are generally **basic**.

A small number of non-metal oxides, such as carbon monoxide and water, are **neutral** — neither acidic nor basic.
groundedIn: Activity 3.8 and the note at the end of §3.2 that most non-metals produce acidic oxides when dissolved in water while most metals give rise to basic oxides.

context: Give reasons.
stem: Platinum, gold and silver are used to make jewellery.
solution:
These three metals sit at the **bottom of the activity series**, and that single fact gives jewellery everything it needs:

- They are **very unreactive**, so they do not corrode or tarnish easily and keep their shine for years. Gold and silver do not react with oxygen even at high temperatures.
- They are **lustrous**, which is what makes an ornament attractive in the first place.
- They are **highly malleable and ductile** — gold and silver are the most malleable metals and gold the most ductile — so they can be worked into intricate shapes.
groundedIn: §3.2.1 (silver and gold do not react with oxygen even at high temperatures), §3.1.1 (lustre, and gold and silver as the most malleable, gold the most ductile) and Table 3.2, which places all three at the least-reactive end.

context: Give reasons.
stem: Sodium, potassium and lithium are stored under oil.
solution:
These alkali metals are **so reactive that they catch fire if kept in the open**, and they react violently with even cold water:

\(2\text{K}(s) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow 2\text{KOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2(g) + \text{heat energy}\)

The reaction is exothermic enough that the hydrogen released ignites immediately. Storing the metal under kerosene keeps both **air and moisture** off its surface, protecting the metal and preventing accidental fires.
groundedIn: §3.2.1 (potassium and sodium catch fire if kept in the open and are kept immersed in kerosene oil) and §3.2.2 (their violent reaction with cold water).

context: Give reasons.
stem: Aluminium is a highly reactive metal, yet it is used to make utensils for cooking.
solution:
Aluminium's reactivity is exactly what protects it. On contact with air its surface is immediately covered with a **thin layer of aluminium oxide**, and that layer is tough, sticks fast and is unreactive — so it **prevents the metal underneath from any further oxidation or corrosion**.

What is left is a metal that suits cooking very well: it is a **good conductor of heat**, it has a **high melting point**, it resists corrosion in practice, and it is light.

The same idea is used deliberately in **anodising**, where the natural oxide layer is made thicker on purpose to improve the resistance further.
groundedIn: §3.2.1 What happens when Metals are burnt in Air? — the surfaces of magnesium, aluminium, zinc and lead are covered with a thin protective oxide layer that prevents further oxidation — with the anodising note in the same section and §3.1.1 for conductivity and melting point.

context: Give reasons.
stem: Carbonate and sulphide ores are usually converted into oxides during the process of extraction.
solution:
Because **it is easier to obtain a metal from its oxide than from its sulphide or carbonate** — the oxide is the form that reduces readily with carbon.

So the ore is first turned into the oxide, by one of two processes:

- **Roasting** — a sulphide ore is heated strongly **in excess air**:

\(2\text{ZnS}(s) + 3\text{O}_2(g) \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} 2\text{ZnO}(s) + 2\text{SO}_2(g)\)

- **Calcination** — a carbonate ore is heated strongly **in limited air**:

\(\text{ZnCO}_3(s) \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} \text{ZnO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)\)

The oxide is then reduced to the metal, for instance with carbon:

\(\text{ZnO}(s) + \text{C}(s) \rightarrow \text{Zn}(s) + \text{CO}(g)\)
groundedIn: §3.4.4 Extracting Metals in the Middle of the Activity Series, which states that it is easier to obtain a metal from its oxide and defines roasting and calcination with these zinc equations.

stem: You must have seen tarnished copper vessels being cleaned with lemon or tamarind juice. Explain why these sour substances are effective in cleaning the vessels.
solution:
A copper vessel tarnishes because **copper reacts with the moist carbon dioxide of the air** and loses its shiny brown surface under a green coat of **basic copper carbonate**.

That coating is **basic**. Lemon juice and tamarind are **sour because they contain acids** — citric acid in lemon, tartaric acid in tamarind — and an acid neutralises a base:

Base + Acid \(\rightarrow\) Salt + Water

Rubbing the vessel with the juice therefore dissolves away the green basic copper carbonate and leaves the bright copper surface exposed again.
groundedIn: §3.5 Corrosion, which states that copper reacts with moist carbon dioxide in the air and gains a green coat of basic copper carbonate — a basic coating, which is what an acid can strip; Activity 3.8 is where this chapter settles acidic and basic character by litmus.

stem: Differentiate between metal and non-metal on the basis of their chemical properties.
solution:
| Property | Metals | Non-metals |
|---|---|---|
| Electrons | **Lose** electrons to form **positive** ions (cations) | **Gain** electrons to form **negative** ions (anions) |
| Reaction with oxygen | Form **basic** oxides; \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\) and \(\text{ZnO}\) are **amphoteric** | Form **acidic** or **neutral** oxides |
| Reaction with dilute acids | Metals above hydrogen **displace hydrogen** from dilute acids | **Do not** displace hydrogen from dilute acids |
| Reaction with water | Reactive metals give the **oxide or hydroxide and hydrogen** | Generally do **not** react with water |
| Reaction with hydrogen | Only a few react, giving ionic hydrides | React to form **hydrides** |
| Nature as a reagent | **Reducing agents** — they give up electrons | **Oxidising agents** — they take up electrons |

The single idea behind the whole table is the **direction of electron transfer**: a metal gives electrons away and a non-metal takes them.
groundedIn: §3.3 How do Metals and Non-metals React? (electron transfer and ion formation), §3.2.1 (basic and amphoteric oxides), §3.2.2, §3.2.3 and the chapter summary, which states that non-metals do not displace hydrogen from dilute acids and react with hydrogen to form hydrides.

stem: A man went door to door posing as a goldsmith. He promised to bring back the glitter of old and dull gold ornaments. An unsuspecting lady gave a set of gold bangles to him which he dipped in a particular solution. The bangles sparkled like new but their weight was reduced drastically. The lady was upset but after a futile argument the man beat a hasty retreat. Can you play the detective to find out the nature of the solution he had used?
solution:
The solution was **aqua regia**.

Aqua regia — Latin for *royal water* — is a **freshly prepared mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated nitric acid in the ratio 3 : 1**. It is one of the very few reagents that can **dissolve gold**, even though neither acid can do so on its own.

That explains both things the lady noticed:

- **The sparkle.** The dull tarnished outer layer dissolved away, leaving a clean, bright surface.
- **The lost weight.** What dissolved was not dirt but **gold itself**, and the man kept the solution. The bangles came back lighter because part of them was gone.
groundedIn: The aqua regia note in §3.2.3, which gives its 3 : 1 composition and records that it can dissolve gold and platinum although neither acid can do so alone.

stem: Give reasons why copper is used to make hot water tanks and not steel (an alloy of iron).
solution:
The deciding property is **how each metal behaves towards hot water and steam**.

- **Copper does not react with water at all** — not with cold water, not with hot water, and not with steam. A copper tank is therefore unaffected by what it holds.
- **Iron does react with steam**, giving the oxide and hydrogen:

\(3\text{Fe}(s) + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \rightarrow \text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4(s) + 4\text{H}_2(g)\)

A steel tank holding hot water would slowly be eaten away by this reaction, and it would rust as well.

Copper is also an **excellent conductor of heat**, which is exactly what a hot water tank needs.
groundedIn: §3.2.2 What happens when Metals react with Water?, which gives the steam reaction of iron and states that lead, copper, silver and gold do not react with water at all, with §3.1.1 for copper's heat conductivity.
